newsitem.title: MEXICO: Three years on, Mexican murder probe stalled.
newsitem.headline: Three years on, Mexican murder probe stalled.

text.p: Three years after presidential candidate Luis Donaldo Colosio was gunned down, Mexicans are dismayed by the lack of progress in the probe to identify those who ordered the killing.
"Colosio, three years and nothing," bemoaned the banner headline of the widely-read Mexico City daily Reforma in its Sunday edition.

The influential La Jornada sarcastically attacked the stalled investigation with the headline: "The Colosio Case in Numbers" - 66 volumes containing 27,347 pages and 127 annexes with videos, audio material and photos.

Among other numbers cited, La Jornada said the investigation had seen 975 declarations, 55 witnesses, 195 experts' reports, 27 lines of investigation, four attorney generals and four special attorneys in charge of the probe.

One of the most disturbing numbers La Jornada reported was 14 other murders allegedly linked to the March 23, 1994 assassination of the candidate of the ruling Institutional Revolutionary Party (PRI).

As candidate of the PRI, which has ruled Mexico for 68 years, Colosio was odds-on favourite to win the presidential elections until his bloody murder at the end of a campaign rally in the northern border city of Tijuana.
President Ernesto Zedillo, Colosio's campaign manager, was catapulted into the candidacy and won a comfortable victory in the August 1994 vote.
But with so little progress made to uncover who was behind Colosio's slaying, there is scepticism in Mexico whether the political will exists to put those who ordered the killing behind bars.
One gunman, 26-year-old mechanic Mario Aburto Martinez, was arrested at the scene and given a 45-year sentence.
But other conflicting theories, including a second gunman and beliefs that it was a political conspiracy in the violent struggle for power in Mexico, abound.

In a poll published on Sunday in El Universal daily, 71 percent of those surveyed said they believed politicians behind the murder would never be brought to justice against 29 percent who thought they would be captured and put on trial.

In the same poll, 63 percent said they thought ex-president Carlos Salinas was the alleged "intellectual author" of the Colosio slaying. Nine percent said the PRI killed Colosio, 5 percent blamed narco-politicians and 13 percent said the government was behind the assassination.

Salinas has repeatedly denied the accusation. He lives in self-imposed exile in Ireland after fleeing the country in shame in early 1995 when his elder brother Raul was arrested and jailed for allegedly being the brains behind a separate political assassination.
"The lack of results from the probe has made people lose confidence in it and the majority of those surveyed are now fed up with so much confusion," Reforma said of its own poll.
